theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A ministry has approved a policy that all business licence renewals must be done online. Marsha Grant is asked to manage its implementation in her agency. What should she do first?
options: Tell staff that paper forms end next Monday
Order new computers for every front-desk officer
Study the policy's aims, scope and requirements
Ask the public whether they like the new policy

questions.stem: What is the main difference between developing a policy and implementing it?
options: Implementing puts an agreed policy into practice
Implementing means deciding what the policy says
Implementing is done only by elected politicians
Implementing ends on the day the policy is published

questions.stem: Which item belongs in a policy implementation plan?
options: A history of the ministry since independence
The staff's personal opinions of the policy
A list of other policies the agency dislikes
Tasks, owners, resources, timelines and measures

questions.stem: A parish council is implementing a new policy on street vending in a town centre. Which groups should it identify as stakeholders?
options: Only the councillors who voted for the policy
Vendors, shoppers, shopkeepers, police and staff
Only the council's legal officer and the mayor
Only the people who have written in to complain

questions.stem: A stakeholder group has both high power and high interest in a new policy. How should the implementation manager treat it?
options: Monitor it and send it a yearly notice
Keep it informed through the agency's website
Involve it closely in key decisions
Leave it out to avoid delays to the plan

questions.stem: Which is the best example of an implementation risk to enter on the risk register?
options: Staff may not be trained by the start date
The policy was approved by the Cabinet
The agency's head office is in Kingston
The policy document has a printed cover

questions.stem: A key risk is that the new online system may fail on the first day of the policy. What is the best response?
options: Trust that the system will work and plan nothing else
Put the policy off for a year without telling anyone
Blame the supplier in advance in a press release
Test the system early and keep a paper back-up ready

questions.stem: Kirk Henry finds that his unit lacks the staff to carry out a new inspection policy by the deadline. What should he do?
options: Quietly cut the number of inspections to fit his staff
Set out the gap and costed options for his director
Ask staff to work unpaid weekends until it is done
Report that the policy is being met when it is not

questions.stem: Why should a policy implementation plan include a budget?
options: Because a policy cannot be read without one
Because every public policy must make a profit
Because resources need approval and control
Because otherwise the auditor will write the plan

questions.stem: Which tool best shows the order and timing of the implementation tasks?
options: A Gantt chart
A pie chart
An organisation chart
A SWOT analysis

questions.stem: Why might a ministry first pilot a new policy in one parish before rolling it out across the island?
options: To avoid ever rolling it out in other parishes
To let one parish write its own version of it
To save the cost of training staff elsewhere
To test the procedures and fix problems first

questions.stem: After a policy is approved, why do staff usually need written procedures as well?
options: Because the policy itself will then be withdrawn
Because procedures show how to apply it day to day
Because procedures remove the need for training
Because staff may then change the policy's aims

questions.stem: A new public complaints policy starts next month. Which training approach is likely to work best?
options: Email the policy and ask staff to read it at home
Train the managers only and hope the rest follow
Run short practical sessions based on real cases
Pin a copy to the notice board and say nothing

questions.stem: Which message best explains a new policy to frontline staff?
options: What is changing, why, when and what it means for them
A copy of the Cabinet decision with no further comment
A notice that no questions about the policy are allowed
A long account of how the policy was debated

questions.stem: A government agency is changing its opening hours under a new service policy. How should it tell the public?
options: Change the hours and let people find out at the door
Tell only the customers who complain afterwards
Put up one notice inside the office on the day
Give notice early through several channels

questions.stem: Staff at a revenue office resist a new policy because they fear it will add to their workload. What should the manager do first?
options: Warn them that resisting a policy is a disciplinary matter
Listen to their concerns and check whether they are valid
Tell them it came from above and cannot be discussed
Move the staff who complain to other sections

questions.stem: Which action most helps staff to accept a policy change?
options: Announcing the change on the day it starts
Keeping the reasons for the change confidential
Involving staff in planning how it will work
Making several other changes at the same time

questions.stem: What is the role of a "change champion" during policy implementation?
options: A trusted colleague who explains and backs the change
An outside lawyer who enforces the policy on all staff
The minister who announces the policy in Parliament
A member of the public who campaigns against the policy

questions.stem: A director delegates implementation tasks to her section heads. Who remains accountable for the overall implementation?
options: The section heads alone, once the tasks are given
The officers who carry out each task on the ground
The members of the public who must follow the policy
The director, who must still oversee the results

questions.stem: A new policy needs a computer system change, new forms and staff training. Which order of work is most sensible?
options: Train staff, then design the system and forms they will use
Design the system and forms, test them, then train staff
Launch the policy, then design the forms afterwards
Print the forms, launch, then decide on the system

questions.stem: Two officers apply a new fee-waiver policy differently: one waives fees for all pensioners, the other for none. What should the manager do?
options: Let each officer use their own judgement as before
Ask the public which of the two officers they prefer
Clarify the criteria and retrain both officers
Stop all fee waivers until the next policy review

questions.stem: A customer's situation is not covered by the new policy. What should the officer do?
options: Refer it to the person authorised to decide, and record it
Refuse the customer any service without giving a reason
Make up a rule and apply it to every similar case
Set the policy aside and do whatever the customer asks

questions.stem: A policy aims to issue birth certificates faster. Which is an output indicator for it?
options: Public trust in the registration agency
Fewer children missing school for lack of papers
Better health outcomes for newborn babies
Certificates issued within five working days

questions.stem: A school feeding policy aims to improve students' learning. Which is an outcome indicator for it?
options: Number of meals served each school day
Change in attendance and test results
Number of cooks hired for the programme
Amount of food bought each month

questions.stem: Why should a manager record a baseline before a policy is put into practice?
options: So that staff know who wrote the policy
So that the plan looks complete on paper
So later results can be compared
So that the policy cannot be changed later

questions.stem: Before a new policy, an agency processed 60% of applications within ten days. Six months later it processes 78%. What is the improvement in percentage points?
options: 18 points
30 points
78 points
23 points

questions.stem: The plan targets 1,200 inspections in the first quarter. Staff complete 960. What percentage of the target was met?
Which monitoring arrangement best suits a large implementation that runs over two years?
options: A single check at the very end of the two years
Regular progress reports measured against milestones
A check only when the media raise a problem
A review only if the budget runs out early

questions.stem: Halfway through the implementation, two milestones are a month late. What should the implementation manager do?
options: Change the milestone dates and say nothing
Wait to see whether the delay corrects itself
Find causes, plan recovery, report it
Drop the late tasks from the plan altogether

questions.stem: A new policy requires all payments to an agency to be made online. Monitoring shows that many elderly rural customers can no longer pay. What should the manager do?
options: Report it to the policy makers and propose a fix
Treat it as the customers' own problem to solve
Hold back the figures until the yearly review
Let staff take cash payments informally

questions.stem: How does evaluating a policy differ from monitoring it?
options: Evaluation is carried out only by the minister
Evaluation counts the tasks done each week
Evaluation is needed only when a policy fails
Evaluation judges whether it achieved its aims

questions.stem: Which evidence gives the most balanced evaluation of a new service policy?
options: Only the views of the staff who designed the policy
Results data plus feedback from users and staff
A count of the press releases issued about it
The number of pages in the procedures manual

questions.stem: Why should the implementing agency report problems with the policy back to the ministry's policy unit?
options: So that the policy unit can take over all operations
So that the blame for problems moves to the policy unit
So that the policy can be improved where it falls short
So that the agency can stop following the policy

questions.stem: Why should the implementation team record its decisions and any changes it makes along the way?
options: To show accountability and support later review
To give staff something to file each afternoon
To remove the need for any progress reports
To stop the policy from ever being audited

questions.stem: A journalist asks a public body for documents about how a new policy is being implemented. What should the manager do?
options: Send everything at once, including staff personal files
Refuse, on the basis that all such documents are secret
Ask a friend in the agency to pass on a copy informally
Deal with it under the access to information rules

questions.stem: Before implementing a new staff attendance policy, why should a ministry check how it will be applied against employment law and the public service rules?
options: So that the policy can be made more detailed
So that the way it is applied is lawful and fair
So that it can be applied only to new staff
So that the staff association need not be told

questions.stem: A new shift policy will change the working hours of staff at a public hospital. Who should be consulted early, in line with good practice?
options: Only the patients who use the night service
Only the hospital's suppliers and contractors
The staff and their union or association
Only the newest member of the hospital board

questions.stem: The officer leading the rollout of a new licensing policy owns shares in a firm that will apply for a licence. What should she do?
options: Declare it and step back from those decisions
Say nothing, as long as she treats the firm fairly
Pass the shares to a relative and carry on as before
Approve that firm's licence first to avoid any delay

questions.stem: What best helps a new policy become normal practice after the implementation team has been disbanded?
options: Ending all monitoring once the team leaves
Keeping the procedures in the team's own files
Leaving each new staff member to learn the rules
Building it into procedures, induction and appraisal

questions.stem: A road safety policy needs action by the police, the transport authority and the parish councils. Which arrangement is most effective?
options: Each body works alone and reports once a year
A joint group with agreed roles and shared targets
One body does all the work for the others
Each body waits for the others to act first

questions.stem: Which content should a quarterly implementation report to the permanent secretary include?
options: A full list of every email sent about the policy
Personal remarks about staff who disagree with it
Progress, issues, risks and actions
Copies of every training attendance sheet

questions.stem: How can a manager best check that staff have understood a new procurement procedure?
options: Have them work through a case and review it
Count how many people opened the email
Ask the group whether anyone objects
Assume they understood if nobody calls

questions.stem: Which evaluation criterion asks whether a policy's results justified the resources used to achieve them?
options: Relevance
Equity
Timeliness
Efficiency

questions.stem: An evaluation finds that a policy is meeting its aims in the towns but not in rural districts. What is the best recommendation?
options: End the policy everywhere at once
Adapt delivery to the rural barriers
Report only the town results to the minister
Move all the rural staff into the towns

questions.stem: A new procedure, applied word for word, would stop the policy reaching its stated aim in some cases. What should the manager do?
options: Apply the procedure exactly and say nothing
Let each officer ignore the procedure as they wish
Raise the issue and seek an authorised amendment
Write a private procedure for the unit's own use

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What one-word term means telling the people affected by a planned policy about it and asking for their views before it starts?
What four-letter short form names a chart that shows who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed for each task?
A policy target is to register 500 households. So far 450 are registered. What percentage of the target has been met?
What two-word term names the document that lists implementation risks, their ratings and the actions to manage them?
Of a J$8,000,000 implementation budget, J$5,000,000 is already spent. What share of the budget is that, as a percentage?
What one-word term describes the people and groups who can affect, or are affected by, a policy?
What one-word term names a checkpoint in an implementation plan that marks the end of a key stage?
Policy results are often split into outputs and which other one-word term, meaning the changes the outputs bring about for people?
A policy starts in 14 weeks. Staff training takes 4 weeks and must end 2 weeks before the start. In how many weeks from now must training begin?
An implementation cost J$12,000,000 and reached 4,000 households. What was the cost per household, in J$?
What one-word term names staff opposition to a change, often caused by fear of losing skills, status or security?
What tool maps stakeholders according to how much power they have and how interested they are? (Three words.)
What one-word term names the amount by which work falls behind the dates in the plan?
A policy is rolled out to 14 parishes at 2 parishes a month, starting in January. In which month is the last parish reached?
A survey of 250 service users finds that 175 are satisfied with the new process. What percentage are satisfied?

essays.stem: The Ministry of Education has approved a policy that every public secondary school must have a written anti-bullying procedure within one school year. As the officer leading implementation in one region, prepare an outline implementation plan.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would study the policy with the ministry's policy unit to confirm its aims, what a compliant procedure must contain and how success will be judged. I would set a baseline by finding out which schools already have procedures. My objective would be that all schools in the region have an approved procedure, and staff trained to use it, by the end of the third term. The main tasks would be: brief principals and school boards in the first month; issue a model procedure and guidance; run training for guidance counsellors and deans in the second and third months; collect draft procedures from schools by the end of term one; review and approve them in term two; and check use in term three. Each task would have an owner and the resources needed: trainers, printing and travel, within an agreed budget. A Gantt chart would show the timing and milestones. I would keep a risk register, with risks such as low staff time and schools falling behind, and plan support for those schools. Progress would be reported monthly to the regional director, and parents and student councils would be consulted on the model procedure.
markingPoints: Confirms the policy's aims and requirements and sets a baseline
Sets a clear objective with timed tasks, owners and milestones
Identifies resources and budget
Identifies risks with responses
Includes stakeholder consultation and regular progress reporting

essays.stem: Explain how you would identify and engage stakeholders when implementing a new policy on vending in a town market for a parish council.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by listing everyone the policy affects or who can affect it: licensed and unlicensed vendors, vendors' associations, shoppers, nearby shopkeepers, transport operators, the police, the council's market staff and councillors, and the public health department. I would then map them on a power–interest grid. Groups with high power and high interest, such as councillors and the vendors' association, would be managed closely and involved in key decisions, for example the layout of the new stalls. Groups with high interest but less power, such as individual vendors and shoppers, would be consulted and kept well informed. Others would receive regular updates. To engage them, I would hold meetings at the market at times vendors can attend, use plain language and local radio, and provide a contact person for questions. I would explain what is changing, why and when, listen to concerns about income and space, and feed sensible ideas back into the procedures. I would record what was said and what we did about it, and report back so that stakeholders see their views were taken seriously. Engagement would continue during and after the rollout, not just at the start.
markingPoints: Identifies a full range of relevant stakeholders
Analyses them, for example by power and interest
Chooses engagement methods to suit each group
Listens to concerns and feeds them into the implementation
Records and reports back, and continues engagement throughout

essays.stem: Describe a communication plan for a new policy that requires visitors to a government office to book appointments online, covering both staff and the public.
essays.modelAnswer: The plan would set out the key messages, the audiences, the channels, the timing and who is responsible. The key messages are what is changing, why it will improve service, when it starts, how to book, and what help is available for people who cannot book online. For staff, I would hold briefing sessions four weeks before the start, give them a short question-and-answer sheet and train them to help visitors book. Staff should hear about the change before the public so they can answer questions. For the public, I would start six weeks ahead, using notices at the office, the agency's website and social media, local radio, and leaflets handed to visitors. I would include a phone line and a help desk at the office for those without internet access, especially older people. Messages would be in plain language and repeated in the weeks before and after the start. I would check that the messages are working by tracking bookings, calls and complaints, and adjust the messages where people are confused. A named communications officer would own the plan and report to the implementation manager.
markingPoints: Sets clear key messages: what, why, when and how
Plans for staff first, with briefing, training and question sheets
Uses several suitable channels for the public, with early notice
Provides for people without internet access
Checks the effect of communication and adjusts, with a named owner

essays.stem: Evaluate the main strategies a manager can use to reduce staff resistance when implementing an unpopular policy in a public body.
essays.modelAnswer: Communication and education are the first strategy: explaining why the policy is needed and what it will mean for staff reduces fears based on rumours. It works well when resistance comes from lack of information, but it takes time and will not satisfy staff whose real interests are harmed. Participation, involving staff in planning how the policy will work, is often the most powerful because people support what they help to shape and their knowledge improves the procedures. Its weakness is that it is slower and staff cannot change the policy itself, so the limits must be made clear. Support and training help staff who fear they lack the new skills, and are essential when the policy changes how work is done. Negotiation with staff associations may be needed where working conditions change, and must follow employment law and the public service rules. Simply forcing the change may get quick compliance but often brings low morale and hidden resistance, so it should be a last resort. A good manager combines these strategies, starting with listening to find the real causes of resistance, and uses change champions to spread support.
markingPoints: Evaluates communication and education, with strengths and limits
Evaluates participation, with strengths and limits
Evaluates support, training and negotiation
Explains the risks of forcing change
Concludes that strategies should be combined after finding the causes of resistance

essays.stem: Explain how you would set up a system to monitor the implementation of a new policy to reduce waiting times at public health centres.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would agree with the ministry what the policy aims to achieve and set clear indicators. Input indicators would track resources, such as extra nurses posted and the budget spent. Output indicators would track activity, such as the number of centres using the new appointment system. Outcome indicators would track the results for patients, such as the average waiting time and patient satisfaction. Before the policy started, I would measure the baseline waiting time at each centre so that progress can be compared. I would set targets and milestones for each indicator, for example average waiting time reduced from three hours to ninety minutes within a year. Each centre would collect data in the same way, using the check-in system's times and a short monthly patient survey, and send it to the regional office by a fixed date. I would check the data for gaps and errors. A monthly report, using red, amber and green ratings, would show progress against targets and highlight centres falling behind, so that support can be given early. Problems with the policy itself would be reported to the policy unit, and the system reviewed after six months.
markingPoints: Sets indicators at different levels: inputs, outputs and outcomes
Records a baseline and sets targets and milestones
Uses consistent data collection with checking
Reports regularly and highlights problems for early action
Feeds policy problems back and reviews the monitoring system

essays.stem: Compare monitoring and evaluation, and describe how you would evaluate a policy one year after it was put into practice.
essays.modelAnswer: Monitoring is the regular tracking of progress during implementation: whether tasks are done on time, within budget, and whether indicators are moving towards targets. It is continuous, done mainly by the implementing team, and leads to quick corrective action. Evaluation is a planned, deeper assessment at a set point, which asks whether the policy achieved its aims, whether it was the right approach, whether it gave value for money, and what lessons can be learned. It may be done by an independent person to give an unbiased view. To evaluate a policy after one year, I would first agree the evaluation questions and criteria with the policy owner: relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, fairness and whether results will last. I would use the monitoring data and compare the results with the baseline and targets. I would add fresh evidence from surveys or interviews with service users, staff and partners, and look for unintended effects, good or bad. I would compare costs with the results achieved. The evaluation report would give clear findings and recommendations to continue, adjust or end parts of the policy, and these would be fed back to the policy makers.
markingPoints: Defines monitoring as continuous tracking during implementation
Defines evaluation as a periodic judgement of whether aims were met and value achieved
Sets evaluation questions and criteria with the policy owner
Uses monitoring data, the baseline and fresh evidence from users and staff, including unintended effects
Produces findings and recommendations fed back to policy makers

essays.stem: A government agency will move all its fee payments to an online system under a new policy. Identify four main risks to the implementation and recommend how each should be managed.
essays.modelAnswer: The first risk is that the system fails or runs slowly at launch. It should be tested well before the start date with real users, launched at a quiet time of year, and backed up by a paper or counter process that can be used if it fails. The second risk is that customers without internet access or bank cards cannot pay, which would be unfair and could hurt revenue. The agency should keep an assisted payment point at each office for a period and work with post offices or banks to offer other ways to pay. The third risk is that staff are not ready to support customers or handle problems. Training should be finished two weeks before launch, with a simple help sheet and a named person to escalate problems to. The fourth risk is fraud or data loss. The system should meet the agency's security standards and the data protection law, with access controls and checks on daily reconciliations of payments. Each risk should be entered in a risk register with its likelihood, impact, owner and response, and the register reviewed at every progress meeting.
markingPoints: Identifies a system failure risk with suitable testing and back-up
Identifies an access and fairness risk with alternative ways to pay
Identifies a staff readiness risk with training and support
Identifies a security, fraud or data risk with controls
Uses a risk register with owners and regular review

essays.stem: Six months into a new policy that closes small rural post offices and moves services to larger town offices, monitoring shows that elderly residents are missing pension collections. As implementation manager, what would you do? Justify your recommendation.
essays.modelAnswer: My first step would be to confirm the facts: how many people are affected, in which districts, and why, by checking the payment records and talking to community groups and church leaders. I would then act quickly to protect those affected while the longer-term solution is agreed, because missed pensions cause real hardship. Short-term measures could include a mobile service visiting the affected districts on set days, and allowing trusted representatives to collect on behalf of elderly residents with proper authorisation. I would report the problem promptly to my director and the ministry's policy unit, with the evidence and options and their costs, as the policy itself may need changing. A longer-term recommendation might be to keep part-time service points in community centres, or to offer payment into bank accounts with help to open them. I would communicate clearly with residents about what is being done. This recommendation is justified because a policy that meets its savings target but harms a vulnerable group is not achieving its wider purpose, and public bodies must treat people fairly. I would add the issue to the risk register and track the results.
markingPoints: Confirms the facts and the scale of the problem
Takes prompt short-term action to protect those affected
Reports to senior managers and policy makers with evidence and costed options
Recommends a sensible longer-term change and communicates with those affected
Justifies the action by fairness and the policy's wider purpose, and tracks results

essays.stem: An agency has J$6,000,000 to implement a new policy. It has planned J$2,400,000 for training, J$2,700,000 for a computer system and J$600,000 for communication, with the rest as contingency. The system supplier now says its price will rise by 20%. Work out the effect on the budget and recommend what the manager should do.
essays.modelAnswer: The planned spending is J$2,400,000 plus J$2,700,000 plus J$600,000, which is J$5,700,000, so the contingency is J$300,000, or 5% of the budget. A 20% rise on the system cost of J$2,700,000 is J$540,000, taking it to J$3,240,000. Using the whole contingency would cover only J$300,000 of this, leaving a shortfall of J$240,000 and no reserve for any other risk. I would first ask the supplier to justify the rise and check it against the contract and the procurement rules for public bodies, since the price may have been fixed. I would look at whether the system's scope can be reduced without harming the policy's aims, or whether some features can be delivered later. I would also look for savings elsewhere, for example by using in-house trainers for part of the training. If a gap remains, I would present the director with the figures, the options and their effect on the timetable, and request approval to move funds or extend the budget. I would not start work on the higher price without written approval, and I would update the risk register and the budget report.
markingPoints: Works out the contingency correctly as J$300,000 (5%)
Works out the increase as J$540,000 and the shortfall as J$240,000
Challenges the price rise against the contract and procurement rules
Considers reducing scope, phasing or finding savings
Seeks proper approval before committing, and updates the risk register and reports

essays.stem: Explain how a manager can make sure that a new policy is applied consistently, fairly and openly by staff in several offices across the island.
essays.modelAnswer: Consistency starts with clear written procedures that turn the policy into practical steps, with decision criteria, standard forms and worked examples, so that officers in Montego Bay and Morant Bay make the same decision on the same facts. All staff who apply the policy should be trained together, or with the same material, and their understanding checked through case exercises. A named contact person should answer questions and keep a log of the answers, which is shared with all offices so that new interpretations are applied everywhere. Cases that fall outside the procedures should be referred to an authorised officer and recorded, so that decisions are not made up locally. The manager should check samples of decisions from each office each month and compare results, such as approval rates, to spot differences that need explaining. Openness means publishing the criteria for the public, giving reasons for decisions and offering a clear way to appeal or complain. Staff should declare any conflict of interest. Finally, problems found through checks and complaints should lead to improvements in the procedures and further training.
markingPoints: Provides clear procedures with criteria, forms and examples
Trains all staff consistently and checks understanding
Provides a contact point and a referral route for unusual cases, with records
Checks samples of decisions and compares offices
Ensures openness through published criteria, reasons, appeals and conflict-of-interest rules

practical1.title: Prepare an implementation plan for an approved policy
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a one-page summary of a policy just approved by a made-up ministry or agency (for example a policy that all permits issued by a parish council must be processed within ten working days, or a policy that a public hospital moves to online appointment booking), with a budget limit and a start date. As a group, prepare an implementation plan pack containing: a stakeholder map on a power–interest grid, a task plan as a Gantt chart with milestones, a RACI chart showing who does what, a budget within the limit given (sums checked twice), a risk register with at least five risks, and a one-page communication plan for staff and the public. Give each member a named role: plan lead (keeps the group to time and assembles the pack), stakeholder analyst (prepares the stakeholder map and communication plan), scheduler (prepares the Gantt chart and RACI chart), budget officer (prepares and checks the budget), and risk officer (prepares the risk register). In a group of four, the plan lead also writes the communication plan. At the end, each member explains their part to the assessor in two minutes. Photograph each stage and hand in the pack once for the whole group.
materials: Policy summary, budget limit and start date from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet and word-processing software, and a printer
Flipchart paper, sticky notes and markers
Templates for the Gantt chart, RACI chart and risk register (optional)
photos: The flipchart showing roles and the group's agreed timetable
The stakeholder map on the power–interest grid
The Gantt chart with milestones and the RACI chart
The budget on screen, with the second check marked
The finished communication plan and the assembled pack
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the pack
Tasks, owners and milestones are realistic and fit the start date
Budget is within the limit, adds up correctly and was checked twice
Risks are specific, rated and have practical responses and owners
Communication plan covers staff first and the public, with suitable channels
Plan reflects the policy's aims rather than changing them
Explained their part clearly when the assessor asked
safety: Use only the made-up policy and data, and keep the work confidential to the group and the assessor
Save work to the Centre's folder and do not share login details
Listen to every member's ideas respectfully and share the work fairly
Take short breaks and keep cables and bags out of walkways

practical2.title: Hold a policy implementation review and report to the permanent secretary
practical2.brief: Your group is the implementation team for a policy that has been running for six months in a made-up public body (for example a policy to cut waiting times at a tax office or to register all street vendors in a town). The assessor gives you a monitoring pack: the original targets and baseline, progress figures by office, a budget report, a summary of complaints and staff feedback, and one unintended effect. First, analyse the pack and work out progress against each target. Next, hold a 30-minute review meeting, run as a role play with an agenda and minutes, to agree the causes of any problems and the corrective actions. Finally, write a two-page progress report to the permanent secretary with RAG ratings, the issues, the unintended effect and your recommendations. Give each member a named role: chairperson (prepares the agenda and runs the meeting), analyst (works the progress figures, checked twice by another member), minute-taker (records the discussion, decisions and actions), risk and issues officer (updates the risk register), and report writer (drafts the report). In a group of four, the chairperson also updates the risk register. Every member must speak in the meeting. Photograph each stage and hand in the analysis, agenda, minutes, risk register and report.
materials: Computers with spreadsheet and word-processing software, and a printer
photos: The analysis sheet showing progress against each target
The agenda for the review meeting
The meeting in progress (work area and notes only if anyone prefers no face)
The signed minutes with actions, owners and dates
